overlays.hook: Her famous arrest photo *isn't from that day.*

beats.text: On December 1, 1955, in Montgomery, Alabama, she refused to give up her bus seat to a white passenger. She was arrested.

visual.title: Dec. 1, 1955
visual.sub: she refuses to give up her seat

beats.text: The driver was James Blake. In 1943, the same driver had put her off his bus.
She was not just a tired seamstress. She was secretary of the local NAACP.
Black residents boycotted the city's buses for 381 days.
In February 1956, she was arrested again, with dozens of boycott leaders. That is when this famous photo was taken.
In 1956, the Supreme Court ruled that segregation on Montgomery's buses was unconstitutional.
That December, she rode at the front of a Montgomery bus.
But she struggled to find work, and in 1957 she moved to Detroit.
When she died in 2005, she became the first woman to lie in honor in the U.S. Capitol.

facts.claim: The famous fingerprint/booking photo was taken 22 Feb 1956, not 1 Dec 1955.
Refused to give up her seat, Montgomery, 1 Dec 1955; arrested.
Driver James Blake had put her off his bus in 1943.
Secretary of the Montgomery NAACP branch.
Rearrested Feb 1956 among dozens indicted under the anti-boycott law; photographed then.
Supreme Court ruled Montgomery bus segregation unconstitutional (Browder v. Gayle, 1956).
Struggled to find work; moved to Detroit in 1957.
First woman to lie in honor in the Capitol Rotunda (Oct 2005).
